title: Advanced Types
description: Mapped types, conditional types, template literal types, and infer — TypeScript's most powerful tools.

challenges.title: Mapped types — transform every key
challenges.description:
What does this mapped type produce when given `{ host: string; port: number }`?

  type Nullable<T> = { [K in keyof T]: T[K] | null }
challenges.whyMatters: Mapped types let you transform entire interfaces at once — useful when modeling partial or nullable states of config objects from external sources.
hints: [K in keyof T] iterates over every key, T[K] is the value type at that key

choices.label: { host: string | null; port: number | null }

challenges.title: Template literal types
challenges.description:
What type does this produce?

  type Env = 'prod' | 'staging' | 'dev'
  type EnvPrefix<T extends string> = `${Env}-${T}`

  type Hosts = EnvPrefix<'api' | 'db'>
challenges.whyMatters: Template literal types let you derive string union types from combinations — typed environment-prefixed service names, metric names, log tags.
hints: Template literal types distribute over unions on both sides

challenges.title: Write a mapped type transformer
challenges.description:
Write these mapped type utilities (no use of built-in utility types allowed):

1. `MyPartial<T>` — makes all properties optional
2. `MyReadonly<T>` — makes all properties readonly
3. `Nullable<T>` — makes all property values `T[K] | null`
4. `Stringify<T>` — converts all property values to string

Then write a function `toStrings<T extends Record<string, unknown>>(obj: T): Stringify<T>` that converts each value with String().
challenges.whyMatters: Writing your own mapped types cements the mental model — and Stringify<T> is a real utility for serializing objects to query params or log lines.
hints: Iterate over every key with the mapped type syntax and add ? to make each property optional — the value type stays as T[K]
Same mapped type iteration as MyPartial, but add readonly before each key instead of ? — the value type stays the same
Iterate over keys the same way but extend each value type to include null as a union member
Iterate over keys as usual but replace every value type with string — the original value type no longer matters on the right side
Iterate over the object entries, convert each value with String(), and rebuild an object from the resulting pairs — use the built-in pair of methods for entry extraction and reconstruction

challenges.title: Conditional types
challenges.description:
What does this resolve to for `IsArray<string[]>` and `IsArray<number>`?

  type IsArray<T> = T extends any[] ? 'yes' : 'no'
challenges.whyMatters: Conditional types are how library authors write deeply generic utilities — understanding them helps you read TypeScript source code for tools you use.
hints: T extends any[] checks if T is assignable to an array type

choices.label: Compile error — conditional types need explicit extends

challenges.title: Write conditional types for deep typing
challenges.description:
Write these conditional type utilities:

1. `UnwrapPromise<T>` — if T is Promise<U>, return U; otherwise return T
   - `UnwrapPromise<Promise<string>>` → `string`
   - `UnwrapPromise<number>` → `number`

2. `DeepReadonly<T>` — if T is an object, make all keys readonly AND recursively apply DeepReadonly to values; otherwise return T
   - `DeepReadonly<{ a: { b: string } }>` → `{ readonly a: { readonly b: string } }`

You do not need to write runtime functions — only type aliases.
challenges.whyMatters: UnwrapPromise is used when typing function wrappers. DeepReadonly is used to freeze config objects recursively — a common pattern for app-wide configuration.
hints: Check if T extends Promise<something> — use infer to capture that something as a new type variable, then return it; if T is not a Promise return T unchanged
Check if T is an object — if so, create a mapped type where every key is readonly and every value is recursively wrapped in DeepReadonly; otherwise return T as-is
infer U inside extends captures what Promise wraps

challenges.title: The infer keyword
challenges.description:
What does `infer` do in this type?

  type FirstArg<T> = T extends (first: infer A, ...rest: any[]) => any ? A : never

  type F = FirstArg<(host: string, port: number) => void>
challenges.whyMatters: infer is how you extract type information from complex types — understanding it lets you read and write advanced utility types in real codebases.
hints: infer captures a type in a conditional type's extends clause for use in the true branch

challenges.title: Build a typed event emitter shape
challenges.description:
Use mapped and template literal types to define a typed event emitter interface.

Given an event map:
  `type Events = { connect: { host: string }; disconnect: { code: number }; error: { message: string } }`

Derive:
- `EventNames` — union of all keys: `'connect' | 'disconnect' | 'error'`
- `Handler<E extends EventNames>` — a function type `(payload: Events[E]) => void`
- `OnMethods` — an interface with a method for each event: `onConnect`, `onDisconnect`, `onError` — each accepting the correct Handler

Use template literal types for the method names (`on${Capitalize<K>}`).

You only need to export the types, no runtime implementation.
challenges.whyMatters: Typed event emitters are used in monitoring agents, log streamers, and Kubernetes watchers — getting the payload types right prevents silent runtime mismatches.
hints: Derive the event name union from Events without listing names manually — the same operator used for all type-level key extraction works here
Handler is a function type parameterized over an event name — use indexed access on Events with E to get the correct payload type for each event

Iterate over EventNames with a mapped type and remap each key using a template literal type that prefixes 'on' and capitalizes the event name — the built-in Capitalize intrinsic handles capitalization
Capitalize<string> is a built-in intrinsic type
